questions.topic: Two instances of one claim compared
questions.learningObjective: Identify two statements that are instances of a single claim.
questions.stem: At the night handover two nurses compare their entries on the same breathless patient and find that both assert one identical claim about her chest.

options.text: Both entries are instances of one claim, so they can be weighed together as one assertion seen twice.
They are two separate claims about one patient, so each needs its own separate look at whether it is true.
options.misconception: treats shared subject matter as making one claim

options.text: They are instances of one claim only if both were written by the same nurse, since authorship decides identity.
options.misconception: believes shared authorship makes claims identical

options.text: They are instances of one claim only when both use the same technical term, since wording carries identity.
options.misconception: confuses shared wording with shared claim

questions.explanation: Both entries advance one assertion about the patient's chest, so they are two instances of a single claim. A shared patient, a shared author or shared vocabulary does not merge two statements into one.
questions.hint: Ask what both entries assert, not what they describe.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The risk a digression runs
questions.learningObjective: Explain the risk a digression runs for the reader.

stimulus.body: Senior sister: I know Mrs Alder had that fall last month, but if we start there we will not get to why she is breathless now. Junior nurse: I thought the fall explained it. Senior sister: It may, but you have to tell me that before you tell me the story.

questions.stem: During the morning handover a senior sister cuts short a junior's long account of a fall, worried the story will lose the ward.

options.text: A digression is harmless because a handover is informal, so listeners will always follow the later point.
options.misconception: assumes informality removes the cost of attention

options.text: A digression is only a fault when it contains facts, so a personal aside never slows a clinical handover.
options.misconception: believes only factual detail can create a digression

options.text: A digression risks spending the reader's patience before the main point is reached, so its cost is attention.
A digression should be removed whenever it is long, because no detour is worth keeping in a record.
options.misconception: treats length of a detour as reason to delete it

questions.explanation: A digression spends attention the main point needs. The objection is not that the fall is unimportant but that it arrives before the listener knows why it matters.
questions.hint: Ask where the listener's attention is going.

questions.topic: A digression that declares its purpose
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a declared digression guides the reader.
questions.stem: A ward manager opens her handover notes by naming the reason for a detour before taking it, and the team follows her more easily.

options.text: By announcing the detour's purpose first, she shows that detours are welcome only when they have been declared.
options.misconception: reads the declaration as a rule about detours

options.text: By announcing the detour's purpose first, she gives the team a reason to hold on until the detour is finished.
By announcing the detour's purpose first, she makes the detour itself the main point of the handover.
options.misconception: confuses the stated purpose with the main point

options.text: By announcing the detour's purpose first, she avoids having to return to the main point at the end.
options.misconception: believes declaring a purpose removes the return

questions.explanation: A declared digression keeps the reader oriented by supplying a reason in advance. That is why the team waits for it, not because the detour is short or declarations excuse every detour.
questions.hint: Ask what the declaration does for the reader's patience.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The work done by a parenthetical aside
questions.learningObjective: Explain the work a parenthetical aside does in a sentence.
questions.stem: One student nurse tucks a short note about the patient's deafness in brackets between two lines of her handover record.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that the bracketed aside supplies a condition for the main account without opening a second account. It records that the patient never heard the call bell, which explains later agitation, while the handover's forward movement continues and the reader's attention is never diverted from the patient's breathing.

questions.explanation: The aside carries a fact that qualifies the main account without breaking its direction. Brackets signal that the fact is subordinate but not unimportant, so the reader holds it in reserve.
questions.hint: Ask what the bracket adds without interrupting.

questions.learningObjective: Compare two accounts by the weight of their qualifications.
questions.stem: Two senior nurses assess the same case file and find themselves persuaded by different habits of hedging, one cautious and one confident.

options.text: The comparison turns on how heavily each essay qualifies its claims, since the same case carries different weight in each.
The comparison turns on which essay is longer, since a fuller discussion must weigh more heavily than a brief one.
options.misconception: treats the length of an argument as its evidential weight

options.text: The comparison turns on which essay names the most senior doctor, since cited authority settles the strength of a claim.
options.misconception: believes quoted authority settles evidential strength

options.text: The comparison turns on how many cautious words each essay uses, since hedging vocabulary marks reliability.
options.misconception: counts hedges instead of weighing the support given

questions.explanation: Weight of qualification means how much the writer is prepared to claim on the evidence available. Length, a cited rank and hedging vocabulary are surface features that need not track it.
questions.hint: Ask how much each writer is prepared to claim.

options.misconception: treats a unifying question as a matter of reader taste

options.text: A single organising question can carry an essay, but only if the question can be settled by the end of it.
options.misconception: insists the question must be closed rather than open

options.text: A single organising question can carry an essay, because every section can be tested against whether it helps answer it.
A single organising question can carry an essay, since a question needs less evidence than a claim does.
options.misconception: believes framing as a question lowers the evidential burden

questions.explanation: An open question can organise an essay because each section either advances or narrows it. The test is not how the question reads or whether it ends in a verdict, but whether the parts serve it.

questions.topic: Three answers weighed as an argument
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether three answers have been weighed into an argument.

stimulus.body: Charge nurse: The bell was not answered because the patient was asleep. Staff nurse: It went unanswered because the side was busy. Agency nurse: The bell was broken that week, as the log shows. Charge nurse: Right. Now which of those do we take forward, and what do we do with the other two?

questions.stem: Three nurses offer different explanations for a missed observation and a fourth weighs all three aloud before choosing one.

options.text: Weighing the three answers means choosing the one that came first in the conversation, since sequence shows priority.
options.misconception: treats order of speaking as order of merit

options.text: Weighing the three answers means judging which best fits the evidence and saying what the others lack.
Weighing the three answers means deciding which one the ward would find easiest to accept at the next handover.
options.misconception: judges answers by how acceptable they sound

options.text: Weighing the three answers means listing all three in full so that the team can decide for itself later.
options.misconception: confuses listing the answers with weighing them

questions.explanation: Weighing is a judgement about which answer the evidence supports and why the others fail. Ordering, acceptability and full recital can all leave the choice unmade, which weighing must avoid.
questions.hint: Ask what each alternative lacks, not just why it sounds right.

options.misconception: treats agreement between instances as pure redundancy

questions.explanation: Two instances of one claim are separate statements of the same assertion, so each can support or weaken it. Repetition is not idleness, and differing wording is not difference of claim.

questions.topic: The risk a digression runs
questions.learningObjective: Explain the risk a digression runs for the reader.
questions.stem: A junior sister begins her handover with a long account of how she once handled a similar alarm and reaches the patient late.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that the digression runs the risk of spending the listener's limited attention on a story that does not bear on the present case. questions.explanation: The risk a digression runs is that attention is spent where it cannot repay the reader. Here the story arrives before the present problem, so the listener must reconstruct why it matters.
questions.hint: Ask where the listener's attention is going.

options.text: The paragraph that declares its purpose can be judged separately, because a stated aim makes the detour more entertaining.
options.misconception: reads a declared purpose as a matter of entertainment

options.text: The paragraph that declares its purpose can be judged separately, because a longer detour needs a longer declaration.
options.misconception: links the need for a declaration to the detour's length

options.text: The paragraph that declares its purpose can be judged separately, because its aim is stated before the detour begins.
The paragraph that declares its purpose can be judged separately, because readers dislike paragraphs that explain themselves.
options.misconception: believes self-explanation is disliked by all readers

questions.explanation: Declaring a purpose lets a reader judge the detour by the job it claims to do. It is not a promise about length, a matter of entertainment, or a substitute for earning the detour.
questions.hint: Ask what the declaration lets the reader do.

options.misconception: reads bracketing as a mark of low importance

options.text: The aside gives the reader a condition for reading the surrounding account, without opening a separate line of enquiry.
The aside is there so that a reader who disagrees with it can remove the brackets and keep the rest of the account.
options.misconception: imagines bracketed material as optional garnish

options.text: The aside is there because the note was written later and the writer had no space on the main line.
options.misconception: explains the bracket by space rather than function

Each heading restates the organising question, so the sheet reads more easily than one built on separate points.
options.misconception: treats repetition of a question as a matter of readability

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Three answers weighed as an argument
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether three answers have been weighed into an argument.
questions.stem: A handover sheet is rewritten so that three possible causes are set down, weighed, and one is finally chosen.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that weighing three answers requires criteria, not preference: each cause is tested against what is known, and the rejected ones are dismissed for stated reasons rather than merely dropped. The final choice follows from that comparison, so a reader can retrace the reasoning and see why the chosen cause was stronger than the two alternatives on the evidence available.

questions.explanation: To weigh three answers is to apply shared criteria and to say why two are rejected. If the choice arrives without that comparison, the sheet records a preference dressed as a conclusion.
questions.hint: Ask what criteria separate the three answers.

questions.stem: Two student essays on hand hygiene each qualify their conclusions, and the tutor asks which qualification is heavier.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would show that the heavier qualification is the one that commits less on the evidence provided. questions.explanation: Qualifications are weighed by how much they hold back. The essay that retreats to what its evidence supports has given up less than one claiming far more than it can show, so the second qualification is heavier.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that a declared purpose functions as a signpost: it tells the reader what the detour will do before the detour consumes time, so the reader can judge the coming material against a stated aim and stay with it. questions.learningObjective: Explain the risk a digression runs for the reader.
questions.stem: One junior's summary opens with a history of the ward since the reorganisation, and the sisters ask for the current picture.

options.text: The digression spends attention on a history, so it risks putting the ward's own history in a bad light.
options.misconception: invents a reputational risk for the ward

options.text: The digression spends attention on a history that does not help the present case, so it risks the thing the reader came for.
The digression spends attention on a history, so it risks making the reorganisation seem more important than the patient.
options.misconception: recasts the digression as a matter of subject weight

options.text: The digression spends attention on a history, so it risks that the sisters will lose patience with the writer.
options.misconception: locates the risk in the audience's opinion of the writer

questions.explanation: The risk is measured by what the reader loses, which is the current picture they came for. Reputation, subject weight and the writer's popularity are separate matters that the digression does not raise.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader came for and did not get.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A digression that declares its purpose
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a declared digression guides the reader.

stimulus.body: Student nurse: I know this bit about the infection check is not what you want first. But it explains why the dressing was left on, so I have put it before the assessment. In charge nurse: Go on, then.

questions.stem: A short detour in the middle of a record is followed immediately by a sentence saying what it was for.

options.text: By naming the detour's function, the writer shows that the detour is more important than the assessment itself.
options.misconception: infers a higher priority for the detour than the assessment

options.text: By naming the detour's function, the writer excuses the order she has chosen, so the order need not be judged.
options.misconception: treats a stated function as immunity from criticism

options.text: By naming the detour's function, the writer admits that the assessment is too thin to stand on its own.
options.misconception: reads the detour as a confession of weakness

options.text: By naming the detour's function, the writer turns it into a support for the assessment that follows rather than a break in it.

questions.explanation: Stating what a digression is for makes it legible as support for what follows, so the reader can weigh it against a stated job. It neither outranks the assessment nor excuses the ordering.
questions.hint: Ask what the detour is doing for the record.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The work done by a parenthetical aside
questions.learningObjective: Explain the work a parenthetical aside does in a sentence.
questions.stem: The same word opens two adjacent paragraphs in a report, and the effect is to make the reader look for the difference.

options.text: The repeated opening sets up a comparison, so the reader reads the second paragraph against the first.
The repeated opening sets up a comparison, so the reader concludes that the paragraphs cover different wards.
options.misconception: infers subject difference from an opening repetition

options.text: The repeated opening sets up a comparison, so the writer has probably run out of other ways to begin.
options.misconception: explains the repetition as lack of alternative openings

options.text: The repeated opening sets up a comparison, so the second paragraph must repeat the first in substance as well.
options.misconception: infers substantive repetition from formal repetition

questions.explanation: A repeated opening positions the second paragraph against the first, a formal device that makes the reader look for the difference. It says nothing about wards, range, or substantive repetition.
questions.hint: Ask what the repetition sets up.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two essays compared by the weight of their qualifications
questions.learningObjective: Compare two accounts by the weight of their qualifications.
questions.stem: Two professional arguments describe the same ward round and both end with a careful caveat, but the caveats differ in reach.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that the reach of a caveat decides how much of the argument it withdraws. One writer restricts the conclusion to the patients observed on that round, while the other qualifies a broader claim about the ward's practice, so the second argument supports less than it appears to and the comparison turns on the scope each writer has narrowed to.

questions.explanation: Weight of qualification is measured by the scope a caveat withdraws. One narrows to the observed cases, the other to a general claim about the ward, so the second supports less than it appears to.
questions.hint: Ask how much each caveat withdraws.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An essay built around a question
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how an organising question structures an essay.
questions.stem: Three versions of one handover note are compared, and only one of them is organised around a question.

options.text: The version built around a question gains coherence, because questions make a handover shorter to read.
options.misconception: reduces coherence to brevity of reading

options.text: The version built around a question gains coherence, because each part can be checked against the question it serves.
The version built around a question gains coherence, because the other two versions must be considered incomplete.
options.misconception: treats one organising method as proof the others fail

options.text: The version built around a question gains coherence, because a question makes the ward's priorities explicit for all three versions.
options.misconception: credits the question with fixing all three versions at once

questions.explanation: Coherence comes from parts that serve one organising idea, which is why the question-led version holds together where the others read as lists. It neither shortens the note nor completes the others.
questions.hint: Ask what each part is checked against.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Three answers weighed as an argument
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether three answers have been weighed into an argument.
questions.stem: A record book lists the reasons for a delay and then, three lines later, states which reason it accepts.

options.text: The final statement turns the list into an argument, because the accepted reason is the one with the most detail.
options.misconception: makes detail count the test of a chosen reason

options.text: The final statement turns the list into an argument, because a final answer is what a handover is required to contain.
options.misconception: grounds the argument in the format's requirement

options.text: The final statement turns the list into an argument, because the other reasons are thereby shown to be false.
options.misconception: assumes a choice falsifies every rival reason

options.text: The final statement turns the list into an argument, because the choice is now made and can be examined.

questions.explanation: Weighing three answers becomes an argument when a choice is made and can be challenged. Detail, format requirements and the rejection of rivals are not what turn a list into an argument.
questions.hint: Ask where the list becomes an argument.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two instances of one claim compared
questions.learningObjective: Identify two statements that are instances of a single claim.

stimulus.body: Night sister: The patient is ready for discharge. Discharge coordinator: The patient is ready for discharge. Night sister: So which do I put in the file, and what do I tell the family?

questions.stem: Two statements made at the end of a shift assert the same thing, and the reader is asked which one to rely on.

options.text: Both statements assert the same claim, so the choice between them turns on the support each one carries.
Both statements assert the same claim, so the choice between them is a matter of which speaker the ward trusts.
options.misconception: makes the choice a question of standing rather than support

options.text: Both statements assert the same claim, so the choice between them should be left to the discharge coordinator.
options.misconception: resolves the choice by role rather than by evidence

options.text: Both statements assert the same claim, so the file should record both and let the reader weigh them.
options.misconception: avoids the comparison by recording both instances

questions.explanation: Where one claim is asserted twice, the comparison concerns the support for it rather than its identity. Trusting a speaker, deferring by role, or recording both avoid that comparison.
questions.hint: Ask what each statement offers in support.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The risk a digression runs
questions.learningObjective: Explain the risk a digression runs for the reader.
questions.stem: An aside in a ward report explains why a particular chart was written by someone other than the usual nurse.

options.text: The aside works by diverting attention, so it shows the writer knew the gaps would be noticed.
options.misconception: attributes a knowing cover-up to the aside

options.text: The aside works by diverting attention from the chart's gaps, so it is a necessary piece of context for the record.
options.misconception: reads the aside as innocent contextual necessity

options.text: The aside works by diverting attention from the chart's gaps, so it makes the reader less inclined to ask who wrote what.
The aside works by diverting attention from the chart's gaps, so it reveals how the ward actually operates in practice.
options.misconception: claims the aside discloses the ward's real practice

questions.explanation: A digression can manage a reader's suspicions by drawing attention elsewhere. That the writer anticipated the gaps, or that the aside is necessary context, does not describe its effect.
questions.hint: Ask where the reader's attention has gone.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A digression that declares its purpose
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a declared digression guides the reader.
questions.stem: Two leaflets explain the same discharge procedure, and only one says why a particular step is included.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that declaring the purpose of a step tells the reader what to look for while they carry it out, and that is why the leaflet which does so is easier to follow. The other leaflet presents the step without its rationale, so the reader must infer its relevance from context, and a step that seems arbitrary is likely to be skipped or altered by whoever is following it.

questions.explanation: A declared purpose gives the reader a reason to perform a step rather than comply with it blindly. Without one the step is merely present, and present instructions are often executed wrongly or skipped.
questions.hint: Ask why the step is included.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The work done by a parenthetical aside
questions.learningObjective: Explain the work a parenthetical aside does in a sentence.
questions.stem: A filing system sorts notes by the author, and readers keep missing the qualifications hidden inside the entries.

options.text: Sorting by author separates instances from the claims they share, so the qualifications become harder to check.
options.misconception: frames the sorting as a general problem with checking

options.text: Sorting by author separates instances from the claims they share, so the file becomes less useful for clinical purposes.
options.misconception: judges the filing by clinical utility rather than argument

options.text: Sorting by author separates instances from the claims they share, so the entries should be sorted by topic instead.
options.misconception: prescribes a different sorting rule as the remedy

options.text: Sorting by author separates instances from the claims they share, so a reader meets two instances without seeing one claim.

questions.explanation: Sorting by author breaks up the pairs of instances that assert the same claim, so the reader meets two statements without seeing they say one thing. The fault lies in the arrangement, not the qualifications.
questions.hint: Ask what the arrangement hides from the reader.
